hook.text: Many habitable-zone exoplanets are tidally locked—one hemisphere always faces the star, the other is in permanent darkness.

buildup.text: The day side could be scorching hot while the night side freezes. This creates extreme weather at the boundary.

discovery.text: Climate models show that if the atmosphere is thick enough, winds can carry heat to the night side, evening things out.

twist.text: The terminator line—the boundary between day and night—might be the most habitable region on such a planet.

climax.text: JWST is studying tidally locked planets to test whether their atmospheres survive or get blasted away by stellar activity.

punchline.text: Eternal day on one side, eternal night on the other. Life might prefer the edge.

quiz.question: Where might conditions be most habitable on a tidally locked planet?
options: Along the terminator line between the permanent day and night sides
On the day side where the star provides maximum energy
On the night side where temperatures are most stable

details.summary: Tidally locked planets always show the same face to their star — one hemisphere in permanent daylight, the other in eternal darkness. Common around red dwarf stars (the most abundant star type), they feature extreme temperature contrasts.
details.whyItMatters: Most habitable zone planets around red dwarfs are likely tidally locked. Since red dwarfs are the most common stars, understanding whether tidally locked worlds can support life determines how many habitable planets truly exist.
takeaways: One side always faces the star; the other is in permanent darkness
Common for planets orbiting red dwarf stars
Atmospheric circulation may redistribute heat and enable habitability

faq.question: Could the permanent night side be livable?
faq.answer: Climate simulations suggest thick atmospheres can transport heat from the day side to the night side, preventing the atmosphere from freezing out. The terminator (boundary between day and night) might have the most temperate conditions. Life wouldn't need Earth-like day-night cycles to thrive.

faq.question: Is our Moon tidally locked?
faq.answer: Yes — that's why we always see the same face. The Moon became tidally locked to Earth due to tidal friction over billions of years. The same process applies to close-in exoplanets around their stars. Eventually, Earth itself may become tidally locked to the Moon, in the very distant future.
